title: Gut, Lungs, Kidneys and Gonads
summary: How the gut tube, respiratory tree, urinary system and reproductive organs form from endoderm and mesoderm.

lessons.title: Gut Tube Regions and Midgut Herniation and Rotation

levels.kid:
Early on, a baby's tummy starts as one simple tube, like a long garden hose running from mouth to bottom. Over time, this tube grows into the stomach and the intestines.

The tube has three parts: front, middle and back. Each part gets its own blood vessel, like three different water pipes feeding three gardens.

The middle part grows super fast. It grows so fast that the baby's belly runs out of room! So for a few weeks, a loop of gut pokes out into the cord, like clothes spilling out of a full suitcase.

While it is outside, the loop twists around. Then it slides back in and settles into its proper place. If the twist goes wrong, doctors can fix it with surgery.
levels.hs:
The digestive system begins as the **primitive gut tube**, made when the flat embryo folds during week 4. Its inner lining comes from **endoderm**, and its muscle and connective tissue come from the surrounding mesoderm.

The tube is divided into three regions, each defined by its own artery:
- **Foregut**: esophagus, stomach, and the first part of the duodenum. Supplied by the **celiac trunk**.
- **Midgut**: the rest of the duodenum, small intestine, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and most of the transverse colon. Supplied by the **superior mesenteric artery (SMA)**.
- **Hindgut**: the last third of the transverse colon down to the upper anal canal. Supplied by the **inferior mesenteric artery**.

The midgut grows faster than the abdomen can hold it. Around week 6, a loop of midgut pushes into the umbilical cord. This normal event is called **physiological herniation**. While outside, the loop rotates around the SMA. Around week 10, it returns to the abdomen and finishes turning, for a total of **270 degrees counterclockwise** (viewed from the front).

When this goes wrong, babies can be born with problems. In **omphalocele**, the intestines stay outside in a membrane-covered sac at the umbilicus. In **malrotation**, the gut ends up in the wrong position and can twist on itself, a surgical emergency called **volvulus**.
levels.college:
Cephalocaudal and lateral folding in week 4 incorporate the dorsal yolk sac into the embryo as the gut tube. The endoderm forms epithelium and glands, and **splanchnic mesoderm** forms the lamina propria, muscularis and visceral peritoneum. The tube is suspended by a **dorsal mesentery**, and the foregut also has a ventral mesentery. The midgut keeps a temporary connection to the yolk sac through the **vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct**.

**Regional boundaries** follow the arterial supply:
- Foregut, supplied by the celiac trunk, runs to just distal to the major duodenal papilla.
- Midgut, supplied by the SMA, runs from there to the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal third of the transverse colon.
- Hindgut, supplied by the IMA, runs to the pectinate line. The cloaca is divided by the **urorectal septum**.

**Stomach rotation.** The stomach rotates 90 degrees clockwise around its longitudinal axis, so the left vagus nerve ends up anterior. Faster growth of the dorsal wall makes the greater curvature. This rotation swings the duodenum to the right and makes most of it retroperitoneal.

**Midgut loop events:**
- Week 6: a U-shaped loop herniates into the umbilical cord. It has a cranial limb, which becomes most of the small bowel, and a caudal limb, which becomes the distal ileum to the transverse colon. The vitelline duct marks the apex. The loop rotates **90 degrees counterclockwise** around the SMA axis.
- Week 10: the loop returns. The cranial limb (jejunum) enters first and fills the left side. The loop turns another **180 degrees counterclockwise**, bringing the total to 270 degrees.
- The cecum then descends from the right upper quadrant to the right iliac fossa. The ascending and descending colon fuse to the posterior wall and become secondarily retroperitoneal.

**Consequences:**
- Failure to return gives **omphalocele**, which is covered by amnion and peritoneum.
- A persistent vitelline duct remnant gives **Meckel diverticulum**.
- Incomplete rotation leaves a narrow mesenteric base, which risks midgut volvulus.
levels.phd:
Anteroposterior patterning of the gut endoderm is set by a gradient that is high in posterior **Wnt, FGF4 and BMP** signals. These promote **CDX2** in the hindgut and midgut. Anteriorly, Wnt antagonists such as Dkk1 and Sfrp proteins allow **SOX2** expression in the foregut. CDX2 and SOX2 cross-repress each other. Conditional loss of Cdx2 in mouse intestine causes gastric-type epithelium, and ectopic Sox2 does the reverse, so the two factors act as regional identity switches. **Nested Hox codes** in the splanchnic mesoderm, together with Shh signalling from the endoderm, help define the sphincters and organ boundaries, such as the pyloric and ileocecal regions.

**Left-right asymmetry drives rotation.** The direction of gut looping traces back to nodal cilia flow, which activates the Nodal-Lefty-**PITX2** cascade in left lateral plate mesoderm. Work by Davis and colleagues (2008) showed that Pitx2 makes left dorsal mesentery cells condense and become more columnar, while right-side cells stay loose. This tilts the gut tube leftward and sets the direction of rotation. Pitx2 mutants show randomized or absent rotation, which links midgut malrotation to **heterotaxy syndromes**.

**Physical forces.** Savin and colleagues (2011, Nature) showed that the stereotyped looping pattern comes from a mismatch between the elongation of the gut tube and that of the attached, more slowly growing elastic mesentery. They reproduced chick, quail, finch and mouse loop patterns with a rubber-tube model and simple mechanics. Rotation therefore reflects an interplay of genetic asymmetry and differential growth, not a pre-programmed twist.

**Herniation timing.** The midgut lengthens rapidly while the liver and mesonephros fill the abdominal cavity, so the loop is pushed into the extraembryonic coelom. Its return around weeks 10-12 coincides with relative regression of the mesonephros, slower liver growth and enlargement of the abdominal cavity. The exact trigger for the rapid return is still debated.

**Omphalocele and gastroschisis differ.** Omphalocele is a failure of the physiologically herniated loop to return, and it is covered by a sac. Gastroschisis is a full-thickness paraumbilical defect, usually right-sided, with no sac. Its proposed mechanisms remain controversial, including vascular disruption of the right omphalomesenteric artery and failed body wall folding.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the embryology matters because of the **narrow mesenteric pedicle**. In malrotation, the duodenojejunal junction fails to reach its normal position left of the spine at the level of the pylorus, and the cecum sits high. The base of the SMA mesentery is therefore short, and the whole midgut can twist around it. The result is **midgut volvulus** with SMA occlusion, which can cause loss of the entire small bowel within hours.

Key practice points:
- **Bilious vomiting in a neonate** is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. The standard study is an **upper GI contrast series** showing the position of the duodenojejunal junction. A classic sign is the corkscrew duodenum. Ultrasound reversal of SMA-SMV orientation and the whirlpool sign are useful adjuncts, but a normal ultrasound does not exclude malrotation.
- **Ladd bands** are peritoneal bands from the abnormally placed cecum that cross the duodenum and can obstruct it. The **Ladd procedure** has four parts: untwisting counterclockwise, dividing the bands, widening the mesenteric base, and usually appendectomy because the cecum ends up in the left abdomen. It does not restore normal anatomy.
- **Heterotaxy** patients often have rotational anomalies. Whether asymptomatic patients should have a prophylactic Ladd procedure is an open, actively debated question, and practice is shifting toward watchful observation in selected cases.
- **Omphalocele** is strongly associated with chromosomal anomalies (trisomies 13 and 18), **Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome** and cardiac defects, so it needs a genetic and cardiac workup. Gastroschisis is usually isolated but carries risks of bowel injury from amniotic exposure and of intestinal atresia. Gastroschisis prevalence has risen over recent decades and is associated with young maternal age.
- Midgut herniation is normal on first-trimester ultrasound. Diagnosing omphalocele before about 12 weeks risks a false positive.

**Frontiers.** Human intestinal organoids from pluripotent stem cells, pioneered by Wells and Spence, recreate CDX2-dependent patterning. When transplanted into mice, they mature into tissue with crypts and villi, offering models of congenital enteropathies. Researchers are also studying fetal surgical approaches, and the genetics of isolated malrotation remain poorly defined.

keyPoints: The gut tube forms by embryonic folding; endoderm lines it and splanchnic mesoderm forms its wall
Foregut, midgut and hindgut are defined by the celiac trunk, SMA and IMA
The midgut herniates into the umbilical cord around week 6 and returns around week 10
The midgut rotates a total of 270 degrees counterclockwise around the SMA
Failure to return gives omphalocele; a vitelline duct remnant gives Meckel diverticulum
Malrotation leaves a narrow mesentery that risks midgut volvulus, a surgical emergency

test.q: Which artery supplies the midgut?
test.explain: The SMA is the artery of the midgut and is also the axis of its rotation. The celiac trunk supplies the foregut and the IMA supplies the hindgut.

test.q: Which germ layer forms the epithelial lining of the gut tube?
test.explain: Endoderm lines the gut. Splanchnic mesoderm forms the muscle and connective tissue of the wall.

test.q: Around which week does the midgut loop normally herniate into the umbilical cord?
test.explain: Physiological herniation begins around week 6 because the abdomen is too small for the rapidly lengthening midgut.

test.q: What is the total rotation of the midgut, viewed from the front?
test.explain: The midgut turns 90 degrees counterclockwise during herniation and 180 more on return, making 270 degrees in total.

test.q: Which structure belongs to the hindgut?
test.explain: The descending colon is supplied by the IMA, so it is hindgut. The terminal ileum, vermiform appendix and proximal jejunum are all midgut.

test.q: A newborn has intestines outside the abdomen in a membrane-covered sac at the umbilicus. This is:
test.explain: Omphalocele is a failure of the herniated loop to return, and it is covered by a sac. Gastroschisis has no sac.

test.q: Why is malrotation dangerous?
choices: It doubles the length of the colon
It blocks bile from reaching the liver
It stops the stomach from making acid
A narrow mesenteric base lets the gut twist
test.explain: A short mesenteric pedicle allows midgut volvulus, which cuts off the SMA blood supply.

test.q: The stomach's 90-degree clockwise rotation places which nerve anteriorly?
test.explain: After the stomach rotates, the left vagus nerve lies anterior and the right vagus lies posterior.

test.q: Which limb of the midgut loop returns to the abdomen first?
test.explain: The jejunum, from the cranial limb, returns first and fills the left side. The cecum returns last.

test.q: A persistent remnant of the vitelline duct is called a ___ diverticulum.
test.explain: Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, which connected the midgut to the yolk sac.

test.q: What is the name for twisting of the gut around its mesentery, which can cut off its blood supply?
test.explain: Volvulus is the surgical emergency that malrotation risks.

test.q: The normal temporary bulging of the midgut into the umbilical cord is called physiological ___.
test.explain: It is normal and resolves around week 10 when the gut returns to the abdomen.

kidTest.q: What does a baby's gut start out as?
kidTest.explain: The gut begins as one long tube from mouth to bottom.

kidTest.q: How many main parts does the gut tube have?
kidTest.explain: It has three parts: front, middle and back.

kidTest.q: Why does the middle gut poke out into the cord?
choices: The belly runs out of room
kidTest.explain: The middle gut grows so fast that it doesn't fit inside the belly for a while.

kidTest.q: What does the gut loop do while it is outside?
kidTest.explain: It turns, then slides back in and settles into its proper place.

kidTest.q: Doctors can fix a wrong gut twist with an operation called s _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Surgeons can untwist the gut and put it in a safer position.

advancedTest.q: A mouse embryo lacks Pitx2 in left lateral plate mesoderm. The most likely gut phenotype is:
choices: Gastric epithelium replacing the intestinal lining
Failure of the gut tube to close during folding
Randomized or absent rotation of the gut
Persistent vitelline duct with a normal rotation
advancedTest.explain: Pitx2 creates left-right differences in the dorsal mesentery that tilt the gut and set the direction of rotation. Gastric-type epithelium would come from Cdx2 loss, not Pitx2 loss.

advancedTest.q: Conditional Cdx2 deletion in mouse intestinal endoderm produces stomach-like epithelium. This best supports:
choices: Mesenteric mechanics setting the type of epithelium
Cross-repressing CDX2 and SOX2 acting as regional identity switches
Wnt signals forming the stomach directly
Hox genes in endoderm being the main driver of organ identity
advancedTest.explain: Without CDX2, SOX2-driven foregut identity takes over, which shows that the two factors act as mutually repressive regional switches.

advancedTest.q: The rubber-tube experiments of Savin and colleagues argue that gut looping mainly reflects:
choices: Contraction of smooth muscle in the gut wall
Different growth rates of the gut tube and its mesentery
A preset twist encoded by Hox genes
Pressure from the growing liver on the midgut loop
advancedTest.explain: A mismatch between gut tube and mesentery elongation reproduced species-specific loop patterns using simple mechanics.

advancedTest.q: A neonate with an abdominal wall defect is sent for karyotyping and an echocardiogram. Which finding most justifies this workup?
choices: A right-sided defect with free bowel and no sac
Bowel thickening caused by amniotic fluid exposure
Intestinal atresia seen next to exposed bowel
A midline umbilical sac covered by membrane
advancedTest.explain: A membrane-covered umbilical sac is an omphalocele, which is linked to trisomies, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and heart defects. Gastroschisis, shown by the other options, is usually isolated.

lessons.title: Liver, Pancreas and Biliary Bud Development

levels.kid:
Inside a tiny growing baby there is a long tube that will become the gut. Early on, the tube is plain, like a garden hose.

Then the tube starts to grow little bumps, like buds on a branch. One bump grows into the **liver**, a big organ that cleans the blood and makes bile to help digest fat. A smaller bump becomes the **gallbladder**, a tiny bag that stores bile.

Two more bumps become the **pancreas**. One is in front and one is behind. Later they swing together and join into one organ. The pancreas makes juices for digestion and insulin to control sugar.

In the baby, the liver even helps make blood!
levels.hs:
The liver, gallbladder and pancreas all start as outgrowths, called **buds**, from the **foregut**, the front part of the embryo's gut tube. The gut tube is made of **endoderm**, the innermost germ layer, wrapped in mesoderm.

- **Liver bud (hepatic diverticulum):** appears around week 4 at the end of the foregut, near what becomes the duodenum. It grows into a sheet of mesoderm called the **septum transversum**. Endoderm cells become **hepatocytes** (liver cells) and bile duct cells, while mesoderm provides blood vessels and connective tissue.
- **Gallbladder and cystic duct:** form from a small lower branch of the same bud.
- **Pancreas:** forms from two buds, a **dorsal** (back) bud and a **ventral** (front) bud. When the duodenum rotates, the ventral bud swings around behind and fuses with the dorsal bud, around weeks 6 to 7.

The fetal liver is a major site of **blood cell formation (hematopoiesis)**, which is why it is so large. It makes up about 10% of body weight near week 10.

A real example: if the swinging ventral pancreas wraps all the way around the duodenum, it forms an **annular pancreas**, a ring that can block the intestine in a newborn and cause vomiting.
levels.college:
**Hepatic diverticulum.** In week 4 the ventral foregut endoderm at the future duodenum thickens and buds into the **septum transversum mesenchyme**. Signals from cardiac mesoderm (**FGFs**) and septum transversum (**BMPs**) induce liver fate, while nearby endoderm not exposed to FGF tends toward ventral pancreas. Competence factors **FOXA1/2** and **GATA4/6** open chromatin at liver genes.

The bud has two parts:
- **Pars hepatica:** cords of hepatoblasts invade the septum transversum and intermingle with the vitelline and umbilical veins, forming hepatic sinusoids.
- **Pars cystica:** becomes the gallbladder and cystic duct. The stalk becomes the **common bile duct**.

**Hepatoblasts** are bipotent. Next to portal vein mesenchyme they form a **ductal plate**, a ring of biliary cells that remodels into intrahepatic bile ducts (driven by **Notch/JAG1** and **HNF1β**). Cells away from portal tracts become hepatocytes (**HNF4α**). Bile formation begins around week 12.

The septum transversum also gives rise to stellate cells and other liver stroma, the liver capsule, the **falciform ligament** and **lesser omentum** (from ventral mesentery), and part of the diaphragm.

**Pancreas.** Dorsal and ventral buds arise near the hepatic diverticulum. Key steps:
- Pancreatic fate needs **PDX1** and **PTF1A**. Notochord signals repress **Sonic hedgehog** in dorsal pre-pancreatic endoderm, allowing pancreas to form.
- Duodenal rotation carries the ventral bud dorsally, with the bile duct. Fusion occurs by weeks 6–7.
- **Ventral bud → uncinate process and part of the head; main duct proximal part.** **Dorsal bud → rest of head, body, tail.**
- The main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) = distal dorsal duct + ventral duct. The proximal dorsal duct may persist as the accessory duct (of Santorini).

Endocrine cells arise from **NGN3+** progenitors. Islets form during the third month, and insulin is secreted by about week 10.
levels.phd:
Hepatic and ventral pancreatic fates are separated within a shared ventral foregut progenitor field. Deutsch, Zaret and colleagues showed in mouse explants that **cardiac mesoderm FGF** signalling, dose-dependently, diverts ventral endoderm from a default pancreatic program to liver. Rossi et al. showed that **BMP4** from septum transversum is required too. Zaret's pioneer-factor work showed **FOXA** proteins binding compacted chromatin at the *Alb* enhancer before transcription, establishing endodermal competence. FOXA1/2 double-null endoderm fails to initiate a liver bud.

Bud outgrowth requires an epithelial-to-migratory transition. Hepatoblasts delaminate through a laminin basement membrane under **HHEX**, **PROX1** and **ONECUT1 (HNF6)** control. *Hhex* null embryos form a bud that does not invade. Endothelial cells are required even before blood flow (Matsumoto et al., 2001), an early example of vascular niche signalling in organogenesis.

Biliary specification is periportal. Portal mesenchyme expresses **JAG1**, activating **NOTCH2** in adjacent hepatoblasts, along with TGFβ gradients and SOX9. The ductal plate forms as a single then double layer, and asymmetric lumens become ducts while unused segments regress. Failed remodelling produces **ductal plate malformations** underlying congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli disease. Haploinsufficiency of *JAG1* (rarely *NOTCH2*) causes **Alagille syndrome** with bile duct paucity.

In pancreas, Kim, Hebrok and Melton showed that notochord-derived activin and FGF2 repress endodermal **SHH**. Ectopic Shh blocks pancreas, so hedgehog exclusion is permissive. **PDX1** knockout (and human homozygous *PDX1* loss) causes pancreatic agenesis, but a dorsal rudiment initially forms, reflecting distinct dorsal and ventral induction. **PTF1A** lineage tracing (Kawaguchi et al., 2002) showed that PTF1A loss redirects cells to duodenal fate. A tip–trunk segregation then follows: tip (PTF1A, cMYC) gives acini, while trunk (NKX6.1, SOX9) gives ducts and **NGN3**-high endocrine precursors. Notch-mediated lateral inhibition limits NGN3, and Hes1 loss gives premature endocrine differentiation.

The fetal liver is a hematopoietic organ from about week 6, colonized by HSCs from the AGM region. Hematopoiesis declines toward the bone marrow from the late second trimester.
levels.expert:
Clinically, foregut bud errors appear as neonatal cholestasis, duodenal obstruction and adult pancreatitis.

**Biliary atresia** is the commonest indication for pediatric liver transplantation. It is a progressive fibro-inflammatory obliteration of extrahepatic ducts, not simple agenesis. A syndromic (embryonic) form occurs in about 10% of cases with polysplenia, situs anomalies and preduodenal portal vein, implicating left–right patterning (e.g., CFC1). **Biliatresone**, a plant isoflavonoid that caused livestock outbreaks, damages cholangiocyte cilia and polarity via glutathione depletion and SOX17 loss, supporting a toxic-injury model. Outcomes depend on early Kasai portoenterostomy, ideally within about 60 days. That is why stool-colour cards and direct bilirubin screening matter. Distinguish it from Alagille syndrome, where intrahepatic paucity, butterfly vertebrae, posterior embryotoxon and peripheral pulmonary stenosis point to JAG1/NOTCH2, and Kasai surgery worsens outcomes.

Pancreatic variants:
- **Pancreas divisum** (about 5–10%): failed dorsal–ventral duct fusion, so most secretion drains via the minor papilla. Its causal role in recurrent pancreatitis is debated; it is likely a cofactor with CFTR, SPINK1 or PRSS1 variants.
- **Annular pancreas**: neonatal double-bubble obstruction, associated with trisomy 21 and duodenal atresia. Bypass by duodenoduodenostomy rather than division of the ring.
- **Ectopic pancreatic rest**, often in the stomach or Meckel diverticulum.
- **Pancreatic agenesis**: *PDX1*, *PTF1A* (also cerebellar agenesis; distal enhancer mutations give isolated agenesis), and especially heterozygous **GATA6** variants, which cause neonatal diabetes with cardiac defects.

Regenerative frontiers draw directly on these signals. Stepwise differentiation of pluripotent cells through definitive endoderm, PDX1+ and NKX6.1+ stages yields glucose-responsive β-like cells (Pagliuca/Melton 2014; Rezania 2014). Encapsulated and immune-evasive islet products are in trials for type 1 diabetes. Takebe's 2013 iPSC liver buds combined hepatic endoderm with endothelium and mesenchyme, echoing Matsumoto's vascular niche finding. Cholangiocyte organoids have repaired human bile ducts ex vivo.

Open questions include what initiates biliary atresia injury in utero and how far hepatocytes and cholangiocytes transdifferentiate in vivo after injury.

keyPoints: Liver, gallbladder and pancreas bud from foregut endoderm near the future duodenum in week 4
The liver bud invades the septum transversum, which forms its stroma, ligaments and part of the diaphragm
Bipotent hepatoblasts form hepatocytes or, beside portal veins, a ductal plate that becomes bile ducts (JAG1–Notch)
Dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds fuse after duodenal rotation; the ventral bud forms the uncinate process
FGF/BMP favor liver; PDX1 and PTF1A specify pancreas; NGN3 marks endocrine progenitors
Defects include biliary atresia, Alagille syndrome, annular pancreas and pancreas divisum

test.q: The liver, gallbladder and pancreas arise from which germ layer's epithelium?
test.explain: They bud from the gut tube's endodermal lining. Mesoderm supplies their vessels and connective tissue.

test.q: Into which mesodermal tissue does the hepatic diverticulum grow?
test.explain: Hepatic cords invade the septum transversum, which also forms the liver capsule and part of the diaphragm.

test.q: Which part of the pancreas comes from the ventral bud?
test.explain: The ventral bud forms the uncinate process and part of the head; the dorsal bud forms the rest.

test.q: What brings the ventral pancreatic bud next to the dorsal bud?
test.explain: Duodenal rotation swings the ventral bud and bile duct behind the gut, where it fuses with the dorsal bud.

test.q: A ring of pancreatic tissue around the duodenum that obstructs a newborn's intestine is called:
test.explain: Annular pancreas comes from the ventral bud wrapping around the duodenum. Divisum is failed duct fusion, not a ring.

test.q: The ductal plate, which forms intrahepatic bile ducts, develops next to:
test.explain: Hepatoblasts beside periportal mesenchyme receive JAG1–Notch signals and become biliary cells.

test.q: Which signaling pair from cardiac mesoderm and septum transversum pushes ventral endoderm toward liver?
test.explain: Cardiac FGFs and septum transversum BMPs induce hepatic fate; without FGF, ventral endoderm tends toward pancreas.

test.q: Why is the fetal liver so large relative to body size?
choices: It forms blood cells in the fetus
It stores most of the fetal fat
It filters urine before kidneys work
test.explain: The fetal liver is a major site of hematopoiesis, contributing to its large size.

test.q: The gallbladder and cystic duct form from which part of the hepatic diverticulum?
test.explain: The smaller pars cystica gives the gallbladder and cystic duct; the pars hepatica gives liver cords.

test.q: Name the transcription factor whose loss causes pancreatic agenesis and which marks pancreatic progenitors (four characters).
test.explain: PDX1 is required for pancreas formation; its loss gives pancreatic agenesis.

test.q: Endocrine islet cells arise from progenitors expressing the transcription factor ___.
test.explain: NGN3-positive progenitors give rise to all islet endocrine cells.

test.q: Bipotent liver progenitor cells are called ___.
test.explain: Hepatoblasts become either hepatocytes or bile duct cells (cholangiocytes).

kidTest.q: What do the liver and pancreas grow from?
kidTest.explain: They start as little buds growing out of the gut tube.

kidTest.q: What does the gallbladder do?
kidTest.explain: The gallbladder is a small bag that stores bile.

kidTest.q: How many buds join to make the pancreas?
kidTest.explain: A front bud and a back bud swing together and join.

kidTest.q: What extra job does a baby's liver do before birth?
kidTest.explain: Before birth, the liver helps make blood cells.

kidTest.q: The pancreas makes a hormone that controls sugar. What is it? (i _ _ _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: Insulin helps control the sugar in your blood.

advancedTest.q: In ventral foregut explants, removing cardiac mesoderm causes the endoderm to adopt which fate, and why?
choices: Pancreas, because liver induction needs FGF signals
Intestine, because Shh repression then fails
Liver, because BMP alone fully induces hepatocytes
Lung, because FGF loss unmasks respiratory default
advancedTest.explain: Deutsch and Zaret showed cardiac FGF diverts ventral endoderm from a default pancreatic program to liver.

advancedTest.q: An infant has cholestasis, butterfly vertebrae and pulmonary stenosis. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Biliary atresia needing early Kasai surgery
JAG1–Notch defect with intrahepatic duct paucity
advancedTest.explain: This is Alagille syndrome: JAG1/NOTCH2 failure of ductal plate formation. Kasai surgery would worsen outcomes.

advancedTest.q: Ectopic Sonic hedgehog in pre-pancreatic endoderm blocks pancreas. What does this imply about notochord signals?
choices: They permit pancreas by repressing hedgehog
They act by FGF-driven liver diversion
They supply hedgehog that induces pancreas
advancedTest.explain: Notochord activin and FGF2 repress endodermal Shh; hedgehog exclusion is permissive for dorsal pancreas.

advancedTest.q: Why is a dorsal rudiment initially seen in PDX1-null embryos?
choices: PDX1 acts mainly in the liver, not the pancreas
The ventral bud migrates to form the dorsal rudiment
NGN3 substitutes for PDX1 in the dorsal bud
Dorsal bud initiation does not require PDX1
advancedTest.explain: Dorsal and ventral buds are induced by distinct signals, so the dorsal bud starts without PDX1, but PDX1 is needed for its further growth and differentiation.

lessons.title: Lung Development Stages and Surfactant

levels.kid:
Your lungs started as a tiny bump on the tube that later became your food pipe. That bump grew and split, again and again, like a tree growing branches.

At the ends of the smallest branches, tiny air bags formed. They are like millions of little balloons. When you breathe in, they fill with air.

Wet balloons like to stick shut. So the lungs make a special soapy liquid called **surfactant**. It keeps the little balloons from collapsing.

Babies only make enough surfactant near the end of pregnancy. If a baby is born very early, breathing can be hard work. Doctors can give special medicine that helps the baby's lungs get ready.
levels.hs:
The lungs begin around **week 4** as the **respiratory diverticulum** (lung bud), an outpouching from the front of the foregut. The inner lining of the airways comes from **endoderm**. The cartilage, muscle and blood vessels come from surrounding **mesoderm**. A wall called the **tracheoesophageal septum** separates the trachea from the esophagus.

Lung growth happens in five overlapping stages:
- **Embryonic** (weeks 4-7): lung bud, main bronchi, lobes form
- **Pseudoglandular** (weeks 5-17): airways branch down to the terminal bronchioles; no breathing is possible yet
- **Canalicular** (weeks 16-26): respiratory bronchioles form, capillaries grow close to the airways, and surfactant cells first appear
- **Saccular** (week 26 to birth): thin-walled air sacs form
- **Alveolar** (late fetal life to about age 8): true alveoli multiply

**Surfactant** is a mix of fats and proteins made by **type II pneumocytes**. It lowers surface tension, the pull of water molecules on each other, so tiny air sacs don't collapse when the baby breathes out. Gas exchange happens across thin **type I pneumocytes**.

Real example: a baby born at 27 weeks often develops **neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)** because it has too little surfactant. Its alveoli collapse, and breathing becomes exhausting.
levels.college:
**Origin and patterning.** In week 4, the ventral foregut endoderm forms the respiratory diverticulum. Mesoderm-derived signals help specify it: **retinoic acid** and **Wnt2/2b** induce the transcription factor **NKX2-1** (TTF-1), while **SOX2** marks the dorsal, esophageal side. Tracheoesophageal ridges fuse into the septum. When this separation fails, the result is **esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula**, often signaled before birth by **polyhydramnios** because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid.

**Branching morphogenesis** is an epithelial-mesenchymal dialogue. Mesenchymal **FGF10** acts on epithelial FGFR2b and drives bud outgrowth. Epithelial **SHH** and **BMP4** limit FGF10 at the bud tip, which makes the bud split. About 23 generations of airways form. The right lung develops 3 lobes and the left lung 2.

**Stages:**
- Pseudoglandular: the conducting airways are complete by about week 16
- Canalicular: the acini form and capillaries approach the epithelium; viability begins around **22-24 weeks**
- Saccular: terminal sacs form and type I and type II cells mature
- Alveolar: **secondary septation** produces most of the adult's roughly 300-500 million alveoli after birth

**Surfactant** is about 90% lipid, mainly **dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)**, plus proteins **SP-A, SP-B, SP-C and SP-D**. It is stored in **lamellar bodies** inside type II cells. By the **Laplace law** (P = 2T/r), small alveoli would empty into larger ones unless surface tension (T) falls as the radius shrinks. Surfactant does exactly this, stabilizing alveoli of different sizes and increasing compliance.

**Glucocorticoids** speed up surfactant production. Insulin delays it, which is why infants of diabetic mothers have a higher RDS risk. Fetal lung maturity was classically judged by the amniotic **lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio**, with a value of at least 2 suggesting maturity.

Fetal breathing movements and lung fluid secreted by chloride channels stretch the lungs. Both are needed for normal growth.
levels.phd:
**Specification.** Foregut endoderm becomes lung through mesenchymal Wnt2/2b acting via β-catenin, BMP4 signaling (which represses SOX2 ventrally), and retinoic acid. Together these set up the NKX2-1/SOX2 boundary. Mouse knockouts make this clear. Loss of Wnt2/2b produces lung agenesis. In **Nkx2-1** null mice, the trachea and esophagus fail to separate and the lungs are hypoplastic. *Fgf10* null mice have no lungs beyond the trachea, as Sekine and colleagues showed in 1999.

**Stereotyped branching.** Metzger and colleagues (2008) mapped mouse airway branching and found three reused routines: domain branching, planar bifurcation and orthogonal bifurcation. This suggests a hard-wired genetic program. Other work emphasizes the physical role of smooth muscle and tissue mechanics. Physical models of the tip-splitting step (FGF10 with SHH and SPRY2 feedback) remain debated.

**Surfactant biophysics.** DPPC's saturated chains let the surface film pack tightly on compression and approach near-zero surface tension. The hydrophobic proteins **SP-B** and **SP-C** help the film spread and reinsert after compression. SP-B is essential: inherited SP-B deficiency causes fatal neonatal respiratory failure. SP-A and SP-D are collectins involved in innate immunity. ABCA3 moves lipids into lamellar bodies, and its mutations cause RDS or interstitial lung disease. Surfactant is recycled by type II cells and cleared by alveolar macrophages, a process that depends on GM-CSF.

**Hormonal control.** Glucocorticoids act through mesenchymal receptors and fibroblast-pneumocyte factor to drive type II cell maturation and SP expression. This was discovered in 1969 by **Liggins**, who saw that lambs given cortisol and born preterm had aerated lungs. **Liggins and Howie's** 1972 randomized trial then showed that antenatal betamethasone reduced RDS and neonatal death. Thyroid hormone and cAMP also promote maturation, while hyperinsulinemia blunts it. Male fetuses mature later, and androgens partly explain this sex difference.

**Mechanical input.** Lung fluid is pushed into the airways by Cl⁻ secretion and held back by the larynx. This keeps the lungs distended, which is essential for growth. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia, oligohydramnios (as in renal agenesis, Potter sequence) and loss of fetal breathing movements all cause **pulmonary hypoplasia**.
levels.expert:
**Clinical translation.** A 2020 Cochrane review found that antenatal corticosteroids for threatened preterm birth (roughly 24-34 weeks) reduce perinatal death, RDS and intraventricular hemorrhage. That last benefit is directly relevant to neurosurgery, since IVH and post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus are the main reason preterm infants need shunts. Steroid use in the late-preterm window (34-36 weeks, the ALPS trial) reduced respiratory support but increased neonatal hypoglycemia. Its long-term neurodevelopmental effects are still debated, and so is giving repeat courses.

**Surfactant replacement** was first shown to work by Fujiwara in 1980. The animal-derived products in use today include poractant, beractant and calfactant. The field has shifted away from routine intubation. Early **CPAP** with selective surfactant is now standard, and **less invasive surfactant administration (LISA)**, given through a thin catheter, reduces the combined outcome of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Synthetic surfactants containing protein analogues, such as lucinactant (an SP-B mimic peptide), are an area of ongoing work.

**BPD as arrested development.** The "new BPD" seen in extremely preterm infants differs from the scarring injury described in older patients. It is a failure of alveolar and vascular growth that occurs when birth happens during the canalicular or saccular stage. Simplified, enlarged alveoli and reduced VEGF signaling support the **vascular hypothesis**, which proposes that disrupted angiogenesis drives the failure of alveolarization. Pulmonary hypertension complicates severe cases.

**Genetic RDS** should be suspected in term infants with unexplained, refractory respiratory failure. Causes include SFTPB, ABCA3 and SFTPC mutations, as well as **NKX2-1 haploinsufficiency**, which causes brain-lung-thyroid syndrome (chorea, hypothyroidism and lung disease). This is a useful neurology overlap. Severe SP-B deficiency and severe ABCA3 disease may require lung transplantation.

**Pitfalls.** The L:S ratio is unreliable in diabetic pregnancies, which is why phosphatidylglycerol was used as a backup test. Lung maturity testing has now largely been abandoned in favor of gestational age criteria. CDH prognosis relies on the ultrasound observed/expected lung-to-head ratio. Fetoscopic tracheal occlusion (FETO) traps lung fluid to stimulate growth, and the TOTAL trial showed improved survival in severe left-sided CDH, though with more preterm births.

**Frontiers.** Researchers are deriving NKX2-1⁺ lung progenitors and alveolospheres from iPSCs, building artificial placenta and extrauterine support systems (the 2017 lamb "biobag" study) to bridge the canalicular stage, and testing whether antenatal steroid courses could be targeted more precisely to the fetuses who need them.

keyPoints: Lungs arise in week 4 from a ventral foregut bud (endoderm epithelium, mesoderm stroma)
Five stages: embryonic, pseudoglandular, canalicular, saccular, alveolar
FGF10 from mesenchyme drives branching; SHH/BMP4 limit it
Type II pneumocytes make surfactant (mainly DPPC plus SP-A to SP-D)
Surfactant lowers surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse (Laplace law)
Preterm surfactant deficiency causes RDS; antenatal steroids speed maturation

test.q: The respiratory diverticulum buds from which structure?

test.explain: DPPC (a lecithin) is the key surface-active lipid.

test.q: Why do small alveoli need surfactant, per the Laplace law?
test.explain: P = 2T/r: as radius falls, pressure rises unless surface tension also falls.

test.q: Which mesenchymal signal drives lung bud outgrowth?

Keeps air bags from sticking shut

Absent kidneys block NKX2-1 expression in foregut
Kidneys secrete FGF10 that drives lung branching
Oligohydramnios removes the mechanical distension lungs need

advancedTest.q: A term infant has refractory RDS, later hypothyroidism and chorea. The most unifying explanation is:

advancedTest.q: Why is 'new' BPD in extremely preterm infants viewed as a developmental disorder?
choices: It reflects failure of tracheoesophageal separation
Early birth halts alveolar and vascular growth
It results from SP-B gene mutations in most infants
It mainly reflects fibrosis caused by high oxygen

choices: Trapping lung fluid to stretch and grow the lung
Diverting amniotic fluid into the stomach
Raising surfactant release from lamellar bodies
Blocking FGF10 signaling to slow branching

lessons.title: Pronephros, Mesonephros and Metanephros

levels.kid:
Your kidneys are like two tiny water filters. They clean your blood and make pee. But before you were born, your body built kidneys in a funny way. It built three sets, one after another!

The first set was like a practice drawing. It appeared near the neck area and disappeared almost right away.

The second set was a better draft. It worked for a little while, then mostly went away. Some of its tubes were saved and reused for other body parts.

The third set is the one you keep. It started low down, near the bottom of your back. Then it slowly moved up to where your kidneys are now. A little bud grew into a branching tree of tubes, like roots spreading in soil.
levels.hs:
Humans build kidneys in three waves, each one lower in the body than the last. All three come from **intermediate mesoderm**, a strip of tissue that runs along each side of the embryo.

- **Pronephros**: forms near the neck in week 4 and disappears within days. It never filters blood in humans, but its duct helps start the next stage.
- **Mesonephros**: forms in the chest and belly region. It works as a temporary kidney for several weeks. Its main duct, the **mesonephric (Wolffian) duct**, later becomes part of the male reproductive tract.
- **Metanephros**: the permanent kidney. It appears in week 5 in the pelvis.

The permanent kidney forms when two tissues talk to each other. The **ureteric bud** sprouts from the mesonephric duct and grows into a nearby cluster of cells called the **metanephric mesenchyme**. The bud branches again and again to form the ureter and the collecting ducts. The mesenchyme forms the **nephrons**, the tiny filtering units.

The fetal kidneys start making urine around week 10. That urine becomes most of the amniotic fluid. If both kidneys fail to form (**bilateral renal agenesis**), there is too little amniotic fluid, a condition called **oligohydramnios**. That leads to underdeveloped lungs and a squashed face, known as the Potter sequence.
levels.college:
Kidney development recapitulates an evolutionary sequence: three successive excretory organs arise in a cranial-to-caudal order from **intermediate mesoderm** (the nephrogenic cord).

**Pronephros (week 4, cervical).** It consists of a few rudimentary, nonfunctional tubule clusters that regress quickly. Its duct extends caudally and is taken over by the next stage.

**Mesonephros (weeks 4-10, thoracolumbar).** It contains true nephron-like units: glomeruli and tubules draining into the **mesonephric (Wolffian) duct**, which opens into the cloaca. It produces small amounts of urine before regressing. In males, under testosterone, surviving tubules become the **efferent ductules**, and the duct becomes the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicle. In females the duct mostly regresses, leaving remnants such as Gartner duct cysts.

**Metanephros (from week 5, sacral).** It forms through **reciprocal induction**:
- The **ureteric bud** grows from the distal mesonephric duct. It forms the ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, and collecting ducts.
- The **metanephric blastema** (mesenchyme) forms each nephron from the glomerulus through the proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal tubule.

Each bud tip induces surrounding mesenchyme to condense and undergo a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition. This produces a renal vesicle, then a comma-shaped body, then an S-shaped body that joins a collecting duct. Nephrogenesis ends around 34-36 weeks, so preterm infants can have fewer nephrons.

**Ascent.** The kidney rises from the pelvis to the lumbar region, rotating its hilum medially, and picks up new arterial supply as it goes. Failures include a **pelvic kidney** and a **horseshoe kidney**, in which fused lower poles are trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery. Abnormal bud branching causes a **duplex system**, and failed bud-blastema signaling causes **renal agenesis**.
levels.phd:
Metanephric induction is a model system for epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk.

The key signal is **GDNF**, secreted by the metanephric mesenchyme. It binds the **RET** receptor tyrosine kinase with its co-receptor **GFRα1** on the Wolffian duct and selects the site where the ureteric bud emerges. Several factors confine budding to a single caudal site:
- **FOXC1/FOXC2** restrict GDNF expression.
- **SLIT2/ROBO2** signaling limits the mesenchymal field.
- **SPRY1** antagonizes RET signaling inside the duct.

Loss of these controls produces ectopic or supernumerary buds, which explains duplex ureters and the abnormal ureteral insertion that underlies reflux. Upstream, **OSR1**, **PAX2/PAX8**, **LHX1**, **EYA1**, **SIX1** and **SALL1** are required to specify intermediate mesoderm and competent blastema. PAX2 mutations cause renal coloboma syndrome. Grobstein's classic transfilter culture experiments in the 1950s showed that this induction works across a filter, which suggested diffusible or short-range signals.

The mesenchyme around each bud tip is organized by lineage. The **cap mesenchyme** expresses **SIX2** and contains self-renewing nephron progenitors. **WNT9b** from the bud stalk, acting through β-catenin, drives a subset of these cells to express **WNT4** and undergo mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition into pretubular aggregates. SIX2 balances self-renewal against differentiation. A separate FOXD1-positive stromal lineage gives rise to interstitium, pericytes and mesangial cells, and stroma-derived retinoic acid sustains RET expression.

Nephron segmentation follows a **Notch** gradient (Notch2 in proximal fates) and a distal Wnt/β-catenin gradient within the S-shaped body. Podocytes arise from its proximal limb, while endothelium invades the vascular cleft. Humans form roughly 200,000 to over 2 million nephrons per kidney, a strikingly wide range. Nephrogenesis stops near 36 weeks when the progenitor pool is exhausted, with no postnatal replenishment. Brenner's hypothesis links a low nephron endowment, from growth restriction or prematurity, to adult hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Epidemiological data support it, but direct counting is limited to autopsy stereology.
levels.expert:
Clinically, these developmental lineages map onto **CAKUT** (congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract). CAKUT is the leading cause of pediatric kidney failure and is detected on routine prenatal ultrasound as hydronephrosis, cysts or an empty renal fossa. Exome sequencing finds a monogenic cause in roughly 10-20% of cases. Common genes include **PAX2**, **HNF1B**, **EYA1/SIX1** (branchio-oto-renal syndrome) and **GATA3**. HNF1B deletion within the 17q12 microdeletion links kidney cysts to maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY5), hypomagnesemia and neurodevelopmental phenotypes. That makes it a teaching example of why kidney anomalies prompt a whole-patient workup.

Useful clinical correlations:
- **Multicystic dysplastic kidney** reflects failed bud-mesenchyme induction. The opposite kidney is followed for compensatory hypertrophy and for reflux.
- **Posterior urethral valves** in boys show that obstruction during nephrogenesis causes irreversible dysplasia. Fetal intervention has not convincingly preserved kidney function.
- **Weigert-Meyer rule**: in a duplex system, the upper-pole ureter inserts lower and more medially and tends to obstruct (ureterocele). The lower-pole ureter inserts higher and more laterally and tends to reflux.
- A **horseshoe kidney** raises the risk of stones and of Wilms tumor and complicates abdominal aortic surgery.
- **Wilms tumor** (nephroblastoma) arises from persistent nephrogenic rests, which are embryonic blastema that failed to differentiate. Causes include WT1 loss (WAGR and Denys-Drash syndromes) and 11p15 imprinting defects (Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome). It is a direct oncologic echo of the cap mesenchyme.

Pharmacology tie-in: **ACE inhibitors** and **angiotensin receptor blockers** taken in the second and third trimesters cause **renin-angiotensin fetopathy**. Features include tubular dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia and neonatal anuria, because fetal glomerular filtration depends on angiotensin II tone. NSAIDs late in pregnancy can likewise reduce fetal urine output.

Research frontiers include human pluripotent stem cell **kidney organoids** (Takasato and Little; Morizane and Bonventre). They contain podocytes and tubules but lack a correctly patterned collecting system and functional vascular perfusion. Newer protocols generate ureteric bud and nephron progenitors separately and recombine them. A further goal is xenogeneic blastocyst complementation, growing human kidneys in animal hosts. Whether nephrogenesis can be extended in preterm infants remains an open question.

keyPoints: Three kidneys form in sequence from intermediate mesoderm: pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros
The pronephros is transient and nonfunctional; the mesonephros filters briefly
The mesonephric (Wolffian) duct is reused for male reproductive ducts
Ureteric bud forms the collecting system; metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephrons
GDNF-RET signaling and reciprocal induction drive permanent kidney formation
Fetal urine makes amniotic fluid; renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios and Potter sequence

test.q: From which germ-layer region do all three kidney stages arise?
test.explain: The nephrogenic cord of intermediate mesoderm gives rise to the pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites instead.

test.q: Which kidney stage becomes the permanent adult kidney?
test.explain: The metanephros appears in week 5 in the pelvis and becomes the definitive kidney.

test.q: The ureteric bud gives rise to which structures?
choices: Loops of Henle and distal tubules
test.explain: The bud forms the collecting system. The nephron itself, from the glomerulus to the distal tubule, comes from metanephric mesenchyme.

test.q: In males, the mesonephric duct develops into:
test.explain: Under testosterone, the Wolffian duct forms the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicle.

test.q: Why does bilateral renal agenesis cause underdeveloped lungs?
choices: The absent ureters press on the growing chest
Missing kidney hormones block surfactant production
The kidneys supply the lung buds with blood vessels
Low urine output leaves too little amniotic fluid
test.explain: Fetal urine forms most of the amniotic fluid. Oligohydramnios impairs lung growth, part of the Potter sequence.

test.q: A horseshoe kidney stops ascending because it is trapped beneath which vessel?
test.explain: The fused lower poles catch beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent.

test.q: What does 'reciprocal induction' mean in kidney formation?
choices: The pronephros signals the metanephros to regress
Bud and mesenchyme each signal the other to develop
Mother and fetus share kidney filtering work
One kidney signals the other to grow
test.explain: The ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme signal each other: one drives branching, the other drives nephron formation.

test.q: Which statement about the pronephros in humans is correct?
choices: It forms the adult collecting ducts
test.explain: The human pronephros is rudimentary, nonfunctional and transient, disappearing within days.

test.q: Around when do fetal kidneys begin producing urine?
test.explain: The metanephric kidneys begin making urine around week 10, which contributes to amniotic fluid.

test.q: What is the eponymous name of the mesonephric duct?
test.explain: The mesonephric duct is also called the Wolffian duct.

test.q: Abnormally low amniotic fluid is called ___.
test.explain: Oligohydramnios results when the fetus produces too little urine.

test.q: The filtering units formed from metanephric mesenchyme are called ___.
test.explain: Each nephron runs from the glomerulus to the distal tubule and drains into a collecting duct.

kidTest.q: How many sets of kidneys does a baby build before birth?
kidTest.explain: The body builds three sets, and the last one is kept.

kidTest.q: What do kidneys do?
choices: Clean the blood and make pee
kidTest.explain: Kidneys filter blood and make urine.

kidTest.q: Where did the kidneys you keep first start growing?
choices: In the middle of the chest
kidTest.explain: They started low down, near the bottom of the back, then moved up.

It turned into your growing heart

kidTest.q: The bud grew into a branching tree of tubes, like the r _ _ _ _ of a plant.

Absent kidneys from failed RET activation
Extra ureteric buds and duplex collecting systems
advancedTest.explain: SPRY1 dampens RET signaling. Losing it lets GDNF-RET signaling trigger ectopic budding, producing duplex systems.

advancedTest.q: Brenner's hypothesis predicts higher adult hypertension risk after preterm birth mainly because:
choices: Preterm infants have more ureteric bud branches
The mesonephros persists and adds extra filtration
Preterm kidneys keep making nephrons into adulthood
Nephrogenesis ends early, leaving fewer nephrons

Fetal filtration depends on angiotensin II tone

choices: Both ureters insert at one site and reflux
Upper-pole ureter inserts lower and obstructs
Lower-pole ureter inserts lower and obstructs

lessons.title: Sex Determination: SRY, Gonads and Genital Differentiation

levels.kid:
Very early on, every baby starts with the same set of parts. They are like a lump of clay that could be shaped two different ways.

Around week six or seven, a tiny instruction called **SRY** decides the shape. It sits on the Y chromosome. If SRY is there, the clay becomes **testes**. If it is not there, the clay becomes **ovaries**.

The testes then send out chemical messages called hormones. One message says "build the boy tubes." Another says "take away the girl tubes." Without those messages, the girl tubes stay and grow.

So one small switch starts a whole chain of steps, like the first domino in a long row.
levels.hs:
Every embryo begins with a **bipotential gonad**, a ridge of tissue that can become either a testis or an ovary. Next to it sit two pairs of tubes: the **Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts** and the **Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts**.

Sex determination happens in steps:
- **Chromosomal sex** is set at fertilization (XX or XY).
- **Gonadal sex**: around week 6-7, the **SRY** gene on the Y chromosome switches on. It makes the gonad become a testis. Without SRY, an ovary develops.
- **Phenotypic sex**: the hormones made by the testis shape the ducts and the outer genitals.

The testis makes three key signals:
- **Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)** from Sertoli cells makes the Müllerian ducts break down.
- **Testosterone** from Leydig cells keeps the Wolffian ducts, which become the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles.
- **Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)**, made from testosterone, shapes the penis, scrotum and prostate.

When there is no testis, the Müllerian ducts become the uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina. The Wolffian ducts fade away.

The external genitals come from the same starting tissue in both sexes. The **genital tubercle** becomes the penis or clitoris. The **labioscrotal swellings** become the scrotum or labia majora.

A real example: in **androgen insensitivity syndrome**, an XY person has testes, but their cells cannot respond to androgens, so the external genitals develop along the female pattern.
levels.college:
Gonadal development starts in the **genital ridges**, which are thickenings of intermediate mesoderm and coelomic epithelium on the medial side of the mesonephros. **Primordial germ cells** form in the epiblast and pass through the yolk sac wall and the hindgut. They reach the ridges by about week 6. Germ cells are not required to decide gonad type, but ovaries degenerate into streaks without them.

**Testis pathway.** SRY (Yp11.2) encodes an HMG-box transcription factor. It turns on **SOX9** in supporting cells, which then become **Sertoli cells**. SOX9 keeps itself switched on through **FGF9** and **PGD2** feed-forward loops. Sertoli cells organize the testis cords. Leydig cells appear by about week 8 and make testosterone, first under hCG and later under fetal LH.

**Ovary pathway.** The ovary is not a passive default. **WNT4**, **RSPO1** (which stabilizes β-catenin) and **FOXL2** actively promote ovarian identity and hold back SOX9.

**Ducts:**
- AMH acts on AMHR2 and causes Müllerian regression in a window around weeks 8-10.
- Testosterone keeps the Wolffian ducts. These become the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle and ejaculatory duct.
- In females, the Müllerian ducts fuse in the midline to form the uterus and upper vagina. The lower vagina comes from the **sinovaginal bulbs** of the urogenital sinus.

**External genitalia:**
- **5α-reductase type 2** converts testosterone into DHT. DHT binds the androgen receptor more strongly.
- DHT makes the urethral folds fuse, which forms the penile urethra. It also shapes the prostate.
- Failure of urethral fold fusion causes **hypospadias**.

**Gonadal descent.** The **gubernaculum** guides the testis down. INSL3 controls the transabdominal phase, and androgens control the inguinoscrotal phase. Failure of descent is **cryptorchidism**.

The ovaries descend less far. Germ cells enter meiosis there and arrest in prophase I as primary oocytes.
levels.phd:
SRY works in a narrow time window. In mice, its expression must reach a threshold within about 6 hours of the normal onset, or the ovarian program wins.

SRY's targets and partners:
- SRY and SF1 (NR5A1) bind the **TESCO** enhancer of Sox9.
- In humans, a key distal enhancer called **eSR-A** lies about 0.5 Mb upstream of SOX9.
- Duplications in this enhancer region can cause XX testicular development. Deletions can cause XY gonadal dysgenesis.
- **Enhancer 13** of mouse Sox9 is also required. Deleting it alone causes XY sex reversal.

The two pathways repress each other. SOX9/FGF9 pushes toward testis, and WNT4/RSPO1/β-catenin pushes toward ovary. This gives the system bistable behavior.

The decision is not fixed after it is made. **Uhlenhaut et al. (2009)** deleted Foxl2 in adult mouse ovaries, and granulosa cells turned into Sertoli-like cells. In the reverse direction, loss of **Dmrt1** in adult testes makes Sertoli cells turn into granulosa-like cells. Gonadal identity is therefore maintained throughout life, not set once.

**Jost's rabbit experiments** in the 1940s-50s showed the role of the testis. When he removed the gonads before differentiation, female ducts and genitals formed whatever the chromosomes were. A testosterone crystal kept the Wolffian ducts but did not cause Müllerian regression. This predicted a separate testicular factor, later identified as AMH.

The **5α-reductase type 2 deficiency** studied in the Dominican Republic (Imperato-McGinley, 1974) showed the different roles of the two androgens. Affected XY infants had ambiguous or female-pattern genitals. At puberty they virilized substantially, because testosterone acts directly on muscle and the voice. This separated DHT's prenatal role in the genitals from testosterone's own actions.

Other genes in the network:
- **WT1 (+KTS isoform)** helps turn on SRY.
- **GATA4/FOG2** and **CBX2** are needed upstream.
- **MAP3K1** gain-of-function variants tilt the balance toward β-catenin.
- **DAX1 (NR0B1)** duplications cause XY dysgenesis. This explains its historical name, "dosage-sensitive sex reversal."

There is a debate about the ovary. The old idea of a "default" ovary has been replaced by an actively specified ovary. However, WNT4/RSPO1 loss in XX mice gives only partial testis development, so other repressors such as FOXL2 must also contribute.
levels.expert:
Clinically, these conditions are grouped as **differences of sex development (DSD)**, following the 2006 Chicago consensus. The three groups are sex chromosome DSD, 46,XY DSD and 46,XX DSD.

The most common cause of atypical genitalia in a newborn is **congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)** from 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2) deficiency in a 46,XX infant. In this condition:
- Excess adrenal androgens virilize the external genitalia.
- The internal structures stay Müllerian, because there are no testes to make AMH.
- The salt-wasting form can cause an adrenal crisis in the first weeks of life. This is why many countries screen newborns for 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

In a 46,XY infant, the hormone pattern points to where development broke down:
- **Low AMH with low testosterone** points to gonadal dysgenesis.
- **Normal AMH with low testosterone** points to a defect in testosterone production, such as 17β-HSD3 or StAR deficiency.
- **A high testosterone/DHT ratio** points to 5α-reductase deficiency.
- **High LH with high testosterone** points to androgen insensitivity.

For a pharmacology-minded learner, two drug links stand out. **Finasteride and dutasteride** inhibit 5α-reductase, which is why exposure in pregnancy carries a risk of fetal genital malformation. Androgen-receptor blockers can produce the same pattern. Exogenous androgens or progestins with androgenic activity can virilize a 46,XX fetus. In each case, pharmacology mimics a genetic condition.

Cancer risk depends on the gonad. In dysgenetic gonads that contain Y material, especially those with high TSPY/OCT4 expression, **germ cell neoplasia in situ** can progress to gonadoblastoma or germinoma. Risk is high in Frasier syndrome and Denys-Drash syndrome (WT1 variants) and in partial gonadal dysgenesis. Risk is lower in complete androgen insensitivity, where gonadectomy is often deferred until after puberty.

Care has moved away from early cosmetic genital surgery. Current approaches use multidisciplinary teams and shared decision-making, and they postpone irreversible procedures where possible. Questions remain open about the long-term outcomes of these choices.

In research, exome and genome sequencing now explain only about 40-50% of 46,XY DSD. Many unexplained cases are thought to involve non-coding regulatory variants, such as SOX9 enhancer copy-number changes.

At the bench, **gonadal organoids** derived from human iPSCs are beginning to reproduce Sertoli and granulosa cell fates. These models allow direct testing of variants of uncertain significance.

keyPoints: The gonad starts bipotential; SRY on the Y chromosome triggers testis formation via SOX9
Ovary development is actively driven by WNT4, RSPO1 and FOXL2, not a passive default
Sertoli cells make AMH, which regresses the Müllerian ducts
Leydig cell testosterone preserves the Wolffian ducts
5α-reductase makes DHT, which masculinizes the external genitalia and prostate
Genital tubercle and labioscrotal swellings are shared starting structures in both sexes

test.q: Which gene on the Y chromosome triggers testis development?
test.explain: SRY starts the testis pathway by activating SOX9. SOX9 carries the program forward but is located on chromosome 17, not the Y.

test.q: Which cells produce anti-Müllerian hormone?
test.explain: Sertoli cells secrete AMH, which causes the Müllerian ducts to regress. Leydig cells make testosterone instead.

test.q: What do the Wolffian ducts form in males?
test.explain: Under testosterone, the Wolffian ducts become the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles and ejaculatory duct.

test.q: Without a testis, the Müllerian ducts develop into:
choices: Uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina
test.explain: The Müllerian ducts fuse to form the uterus and upper vagina, and their unfused parts become the uterine tubes. Ovaries come from the gonad, not the ducts.

test.q: Which hormone mainly masculinizes the external genitalia?
test.explain: DHT, made from testosterone by 5α-reductase, drives fusion of the urethral folds and formation of the scrotum. AMH acts only on the Müllerian ducts.

test.q: In females, the genital tubercle becomes the:
test.explain: The genital tubercle forms the penis in males and the clitoris in females. The labia majora come from the labioscrotal swellings.

test.q: An XY person with testes whose cells cannot respond to androgens most likely has:
test.explain: In androgen insensitivity, testes form and make AMH and testosterone, but the androgen receptor does not work. The external genitals therefore follow the female pattern.

test.q: Failure of the urethral folds to fuse causes:
test.explain: Hypospadias is incomplete fusion of the urethral folds, so the urethral opening sits on the underside of the penis. Cryptorchidism is a failure of testicular descent.

test.q: Which structure guides the testis during its descent?
test.explain: The gubernaculum guides descent, under control of INSL3 and then androgens.

test.q: Testosterone is converted to DHT by the enzyme 5α-___.
test.explain: 5α-reductase type 2 converts testosterone into the more potent androgen DHT.

test.q: What is the term for an undescended testis?
test.explain: Cryptorchidism is the failure of the testis to descend into the scrotum.

test.q: Primordial germ cells reach the genital ___ by about week 6.
test.explain: The genital ridges, derived from intermediate mesoderm and coelomic epithelium, receive the migrating germ cells.

kidTest.q: What does the SRY switch help build?
kidTest.explain: SRY tells the gonad to become testes.

kidTest.q: Where is the SRY switch found?
kidTest.explain: SRY sits on the Y chromosome.

kidTest.q: At the very start, how are babies' parts?
kidTest.explain: Everyone starts with the same parts, like clay that can be shaped two ways.

kidTest.q: What do testes send out to shape the body?
kidTest.explain: Hormones are the chemical messages that shape the tubes and other parts.

kidTest.q: Without SRY, the gonad becomes an o _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Without SRY, the gonad becomes an ovary.

advancedTest.q: Jost's experiment of placing a testosterone crystal on a castrated embryo kept the Wolffian ducts but not Müllerian regression. This implied:
choices: Testosterone acts mainly on the external genitalia, not on the ducts
A separate testicular factor causes Müllerian duct regression
The Wolffian ducts form normally without any hormone signal
The Müllerian ducts depend on estrogen to persist
advancedTest.explain: Testosterone alone could not regress the Müllerian ducts, so another testicular factor had to exist. It was later identified as AMH.

advancedTest.q: Deleting Foxl2 in adult mouse ovaries turns granulosa cells into Sertoli-like cells. The key conclusion is:
choices: Germ cells decide what the supporting cells become
Ovarian identity arises passively by default
Gonadal fate needs continuous active maintenance
SRY is expressed again in adult ovaries
advancedTest.explain: Gonadal identity is not fixed after the embryonic decision. FOXL2 keeps repressing the SOX9 program throughout adult life.

advancedTest.q: A 46,XY infant has normal AMH but low testosterone. The most likely site of the defect is:
advancedTest.explain: Normal AMH means Sertoli cells, and so a testis, are present, which argues against gonadal dysgenesis. Low testosterone then points to a block in steroid synthesis, such as 17β-HSD3 deficiency.

advancedTest.q: Why did XY individuals with 5α-reductase deficiency virilize at puberty?
choices: Testosterone itself can drive many pubertal changes
Adrenal estrogens rose and took over the androgen role
SRY expression increased sharply during adolescence
Their testes began producing AMH again at puberty
advancedTest.explain: DHT is critical for prenatal genital formation, but high pubertal testosterone acts directly on the androgen receptor in muscle and the larynx.
